paragraphs.source_en: Spears and great war blades rose toward the sky, and the massive iron gate, weighing fully five hundred kan, swung open. “Follow me!” Ieyasu shouted. Mototada, Heihachirō, and Koheita followed close behind, galloping out of the castle through the dense morning mist.

paragraphs.source_en: No matter how infinitely merciful Amida Buddha might be, no rice could possibly be harvested from fields that were not cultivated. And without rice, hunger was inevitable. There were rumors that lotus blossoms had fallen from heaven, but Hanzō had never heard of rice falling from the sky; indeed, he had never seen even those lotus blossoms with his own eyes. Seen in that light, perhaps Hannojō’s claim that the Buddha’s radiance shone behind Ieyasu was not nonsense after all.

paragraphs.source_en: Hanzō bent low and squeezed through a hedge of podocarp trees. Smelling horse dung, he realized that he had emerged behind a stable. He hurriedly straightened up and saw a pair of horse’s hooves before the kitchen hearth. His gaze traveled upward along the horse’s legs. A familiar whip came into view—Ieyasu was sitting astride the horse, briskly eating rice steeped in soup. Below him stood a fair-complexioned woman: Tadayo’s wife.
